summary: This best current practice gives guidelines for authors and reviewers of specifications that contain YANG data models, including IANA-maintained modules. It aims to improve interoperability and usability of NETCONF and RESTCONF. It obsoletes RFC 8407 and updates RFC 8126.

plainLanguage.summary: YANG is the language used to describe the data a network device can be configured with and read back. The language specification leaves many choices open, so two modules can be written in very different ways and still both be valid. This document tells authors and reviewers which choices to make, so that modules from different teams fit together.

subtitle: The rules that make a YANG module readable, interoperable and reviewable, for the people who write and review them.

tldr.problem: The YANG specification only defines a minimum level of conformance, and many of its constructs are optional, so two modules written by different authors can behave in ways that are hard to predict. Some YANG constructs, such as infinite-length identifiers or mandatory top-level nodes, are ones no server has to support.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out what a document containing YANG must contain, how the module itself must be written, and which constructs are allowed in an IETF module, with templates for the security section, the IANA considerations and the module code.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 8407, updates RFC 8126 with guidance for RFCs that define IANA-maintained YANG modules, and adds a template and a review checklist.

facts.value: ietf- for IETF modules, iana- for IANA-maintained modules

today: RFC 9907 is a Best Current Practice, BCP 216, published in March 2026. It obsoletes RFC 8407 and updates RFC 8126 with guidance for writing the IANA considerations of RFCs that define IANA-maintained YANG modules, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What This Document Is For
sections.content:
The standardization of network configuration interfaces for use with network configuration management protocols, such as the Network Configuration Protocol and RESTCONF, requires a modular set of data models that can be reused and extended over time.

This document defines a set of guidelines for documents containing YANG 1.1 and YANG 1.0 data models, including IANA-maintained YANG modules. YANG is used to define the data structures, protocol operations and notification content used within a NETCONF or RESTCONF server. YANG is also used to define abstract data structures. A NETCONF or RESTCONF server that supports a particular YANG module will support client NETCONF or RESTCONF operation requests, as indicated by the specific content defined in the YANG module.

Many YANG constructs are defined as optional to use, such as the description statement. However, in order to make YANG modules more readable and interoperable, it is desirable to define a set of descriptive usage guidelines that entails a higher level of compliance than the minimum level defined in the YANG specification.

In addition, YANG allows constructs such as infinite length identifiers and string values, or top-level mandatory nodes, that a compliant server is not required to support. Only constructs that all servers are required to support can be used in IETF YANG modules.

The guidelines are intended to be used by authors and reviewers to improve the readability and interoperability of published YANG data models, and they can be used independently of the IETF Stream of publication or even by other organizations. YANG 1.0 modules have to conform to RFC 6020 while YANG 1.1 modules have to conform to RFC 7950; this document adds usage guidelines in addition to these RFCs. It is not a YANG tutorial, and the reader is expected to know the data modeling language before applying the guidance.

This document obsoletes RFC 8407, and Section 4.30.3 updates RFC 8126 by providing guidance for writing the IANA Considerations sections for RFCs that specify IANA-maintained YANG modules. The list of changes since RFC 8407 is long: errata reports were implemented, the terminology was updated, the file name after the code tag became mandatory, a template marker for the security template was added, a template for IANA registrations was added, guidance on folding examples was added, tool validation checks were added for the line limits of a draft and for JSON-encoded examples, the terms YANG module and YANG data model were given a usage guideline of their own, a section on defining standard tags was added, a section on the classification of YANG modules was added, and a template for IANA-maintained YANG modules was added.
sections.plainLanguage: YANG itself only sets a floor. This document raises that floor for IETF modules: it says which constructs to avoid, how to name things, and what a document containing a module must contain. It replaces the earlier edition of the same guidance.

sections.title: The Terms It Uses
sections.content:
The document defines a small set of terms of its own. Some of the templates use a double hyphen to mark instructions to authors, and text prefixed with that must not be copied as such; for YANG templates, a double slash is used for the same purpose. The term RFC IIII is used to refer to an RFC that defines an initial version of an IANA-maintained YANG module.

  • An IANA-maintained YANG module is a YANG module that is maintained by IANA and has an IANA registry associated with it, such as the IANA tunnel type module. Once an IANA-maintained module is initialized, new values are not added to the module directly; they are added to the companion registry instead.
  • An IETF module is a YANG module published by the IETF that is not maintained by IANA.
  • Published means a stable release of a module or submodule, such as the Request for Comments Series. Unpublished means an unstable release, such as an Internet-Draft, which is subject to change at any time.
  • A YANG fragment is a set of YANG statements not intended to represent a complete module or submodule; the invalid syntax with three dots is sometimes used to indicate that more statements would be present in a real module.
  • A YANG tree diagram is a diagram representing the contents of a YANG module, as defined in RFC 8340.

The document also draws a distinction that YANG itself makes. A data model describes how data is represented and accessed, and YANG structures data models into modules for ease of use. A module defines hierarchies of schema nodes to make a self-contained and compilable block of YANG definitions and inclusions. A YANG module is typically a single file starting with a module statement, may include any number of submodules stored in separate files starting with a submodule statement, and regardless of the presence of submodules the module and its submodules are externally viewed as a single YANG module. A YANG data model can consist of a single YANG module or of multiple YANG modules.
sections.plainLanguage: The document separates the model, which is the idea of how data is represented, from the module, which is the file that holds it. It also separates modules IETF publishes from modules IANA maintains on behalf of a registry.

sections.title: What the Document Must Contain
sections.content:
The following sections MUST be present in an Internet-Draft or RFC containing a YANG module: the narrative sections and a definitions section. Additional YANG-specific considerations MUST be included for the Security Considerations, IANA Considerations and References sections.

There are three usage scenarios for YANG that can appear in such a document: a normative module or submodule, an example module or submodule, and an example YANG fragment that is not part of any module. The guidelines refer mainly to the first, but may apply to the others as well.

The module description statement MUST contain a reference to the latest approved IETF Trust copyright statement. Each normative YANG module or submodule is considered to be a code component, and the strings that mark the beginning and the end of code MUST be used to identify each code component. The opening tag MUST be followed by a string identifying the file name specified in Section 5.2 of RFC 7950, and the name string form that includes the revision date SHOULD be used, with the revision date matching the date used in the most recent revision of the module. Example modules are not code components: the code tag convention MUST NOT be used for them, but they MUST be validated, and they SHOULD be named with the term example followed by a hyphen and a descriptive name.

A terminology section MUST be present if any terms are defined in the document or imported from other documents. YANG tree diagrams SHOULD be included to help readers understand the module structure; diagrams longer than one page SHOULD be included in an appendix rather than the main body, and an informative reference to the YANG tree diagrams specification MUST be included.

The narrative sections MUST include an overview section that describes the scope and field of application of the data model or models and their relationship to other standards. If the module imports definitions from other modules or is always implemented in conjunction with other modules, those facts MUST be noted in the overview section, as must any special interpretations of definitions in other modules. If the document contains major NMDA exceptions or includes a temporary non-NMDA module, the Introduction section SHOULD mention this with the reasoning that motivated the design.

The definitions section contains the modules defined by the specification. These SHOULD be written using YANG 1.1 syntax; YANG 1.0 syntax MAY be used if no YANG 1.1 constructs or semantics are needed; and if any of the imported modules use YANG 1.1, the module MUST be written using YANG 1.1. A YIN version of the module MAY also be present. If the module itself is normative rather than an example, all YANG statements within it are considered normative, and the key words of RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 apply to its description statements exactly as they would in any other normative section. Example modules and example fragments MUST NOT contain any normative text, including the RFC 2119 key words.
sections.plainLanguage: A document with a YANG module has to have narrative sections, a definitions section, and proper security, IANA and references sections. The module itself is marked as a code component with its file name, and anything in an example module is not normative.

sections.title: The Security Considerations Section
sections.content:
Each specification that defines one or more modules MUST contain a section that discusses security considerations relevant to those modules. Unless the modules comply with RFC 8791 or define YANG extensions such as RFC 7952, the security section MUST be modeled after the latest approved template, and authors MUST check the web page for that template in case a more recent version is available.

In particular, writable data nodes that could be especially disruptive if abused MUST be explicitly listed by name, and the associated security risks MUST be explained. Readable data nodes that contain especially sensitive information or that raise significant privacy concerns MUST be explicitly listed by name, with the reasons explained. Operations, that is YANG rpc statements, that are potentially harmful to system behaviour or that raise significant privacy concerns MUST be explicitly listed by name, with the reasons explained.

The template also covers reusable groupings taken from other modules, reminding the reader that the nodes may be sensitive or vulnerable and pointing to the security considerations of the document that defines them. Documents that exclusively define modules that follow the extension in RFC 8791 are not required to include the template, and the same is true of modules that define YANG extensions such as RFC 7952.

The document's own security section states that it defines guidelines for NETCONF or RESTCONF content defined with the YANG data modeling language and does not introduce any new or increased security risks. Its operational considerations section adds that the document does not define a protocol or a protocol extension, so there are no new operations or manageability requirements introduced by it.
sections.plainLanguage: The security section of a YANG document is not a formality. It has to name the writable and readable parts of the model that are dangerous or private, and the operations that could harm the system, and say why each one is a risk.

sections.title: Writing the Module Itself
sections.content:
Modules in IETF Standards Track specifications MUST comply with all syntactic and semantic requirements of YANG 1.1. The usage guidelines supplement the YANG specification, which is intended to define a minimum set of conformance requirements, and only guidelines that clarify or restrict that minimum are included.

Naming. Normative modules MUST be named according to the guidelines in the IANA Considerations section of RFC 6020. A distinctive word or abbreviation, such as a protocol name or working group abbreviation, SHOULD be used in the module name, and the same word should be reused when new definitions extend an existing module. All published module names MUST be unique, and once a module name is published it MUST NOT be reused, even if the RFC containing it is reclassified as Historic, because a module name cannot be changed in YANG and a change would be treated as a new module. All normative YANG modules published by the IETF MUST begin with the prefix ietf-, all IANA-maintained modules MUST begin with iana-, another standards organization might use ieee-, and example modules SHOULD be named with the prefix example-.

Prefixes. Prefixes are never used for built-in data types and YANG keywords; a prefix MUST be used for any extension statement; and the proper module prefix MUST be used for identifiers imported from other modules and included from a submodule. The local module prefix SHOULD be used instead of no prefix in path expressions, and MUST be used in default statements for identityref or instance-identifier data types. Prefix values SHOULD be short but meaningful, and SHOULD NOT conflict with known modules that have been previously published. Prefix values of example modules SHOULD be prefixed with ex or a similar pattern.

Identifiers. All YANG identifiers in published modules MUST be between 1 and 64 characters in length. Identifiers SHOULD follow a consistent naming pattern, and only lowercase letters, numbers and dashes SHOULD be used; uppercase characters, the period and the underscore MAY be used when an identifier represents a well-known value that uses them. Identifiers SHOULD include complete words or well-known acronyms, child nodes within a container or list SHOULD NOT replicate the parent identifier, and list identifiers SHOULD be singular with the surrounding container name plural. Identifiers SHOULD NOT carry any special semantics that identify data modelling properties: naming an object config or state does not change whether it is configuration data or state data, because only YANG statements and extension statements can assign such semantics in a machine-readable way.

Defaults. Substatements containing very common default values SHOULD NOT be present, because using them everywhere would make the module difficult to read. The statements listed in the document's table are config with the value true, mandatory with false, max-elements with unbounded, min-elements with 0, ordered-by with system, status with current and yin-element with false.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for the module file are about predictability: one way to name a module, one way to write a prefix, one style for identifiers, and no repetition of defaults that every server already assumes.

sections.title: Constraints: must, when and augment
sections.content:
The must and when statements are used to provide cross-object referential tests, and they have very different behaviour. The when statement causes data node instances to be silently deleted as soon as the condition becomes false, and a false when statement is not considered to be an error. It SHOULD be used together with augment or uses statements to achieve conditional model composition, and the condition SHOULD be based on static properties of the augmented entry, such as list key leaves.

The must statement causes a datastore validation error if the condition is false. It SHOULD be used for enforcing parameter value restrictions that involve more than one data node, for example that an end-time parameter must be after the start-time parameter. The min-elements and max-elements statements can control how many list or leaf-list instances are required; YANG constraint statements SHOULD be used to identify conditions that apply to all implementations of the data model, while platform-specific limitations should be expressed as a data definition statement, such as a max-ports leaf.

The augment statement defines data definition statements that are added as child nodes of a target data node, and the module namespace of these nodes is the augmenting module rather than the augmented module. A top-level augment statement SHOULD NOT be used if the target data node is in the same module or submodule as the augment statement; the data definition statements SHOULD be added inline instead. An augment is often used with a when or if-feature statement to make the augmentation conditional on some part of the model.

YANG has specific rules about how configuration data can be updated in new releases of a module, and these rules allow an old client to continue interoperating with a new server. If data nodes are added to an existing entry, the old client MUST NOT be required to provide any mandatory parameters that were not in the original module definition. A conditional augment can contain mandatory objects only if the condition is false, unless the client explicitly requests them. Only a conditional augment that uses the when statement form of condition can be used in this manner, because the YANG features enabled on the server cannot be controlled by the client in any way, so it is not safe to add mandatory augmenting data nodes based on an if-feature statement. The XPath when condition MUST NOT reference data outside of the target data node, because the client does not have any control over that external data.
sections.plainLanguage: Two keywords look similar and behave very differently. When a condition stops being true, the data under it quietly disappears. Must, by contrast, is an error the server refuses to accept. The document also spells out how a new module version can add new mandatory data without breaking clients that only know the older version.

sections.title: Lifecycle and Stability
sections.content:
The YANG status statement MUST be present within a definition if its value is deprecated or obsolete. The status SHOULD NOT be changed from current directly to obsolete, and an object SHOULD be available for at least one year after the publication date with a deprecated status before it is changed to obsolete.

The module or submodule name MUST NOT be changed once the document containing it is published, and the module namespace URI value MUST NOT be changed either. The revision date substatement within an import or include statement SHOULD be present if any groupings are used from the external module or submodule. If submodules are used, the document containing the main module MUST be updated so that the main module revision date is equal to or more recent than the revision date of any submodule that it includes, directly or indirectly.

Definitions for future use SHOULD NOT be specified in a module: the document tells authors not to define placeholder objects such as a reserved leaf with a description saying that a future revision might give it a purpose. For published modules, the namespace MUST be a globally unique URI, usually assigned by IANA. The organization statement MUST be present, and for a Standards Track document it SHOULD be the IETF working group chartered to write the document. The contact statement MUST be present.
sections.plainLanguage: Once a module is published, its name, its namespace and the meaning of its identifiers are fixed, because a server and a client that disagree about them cannot talk. A deprecated item stays deprecated for at least a year before it is withdrawn, and placeholders are not allowed.

sections.title: IANA-Maintained YANG Modules
sections.content:
IANA maintains a set of registries that are key for interoperability. The content of these registries is usually available in several formats, and there was some confusion in the past about whether the content of some registries depends on a specific representation format. Section 5 of RFC 8892 was published to clarify that MIB and YANG modules are merely additional formats in which the interface types and tunnel types registries are available: they are not separate registries, and the same values are always present in all formats of the same registry.

A design in which a YANG module includes parameters and values directly, in a module that is not maintained by IANA, while these are also populated in an IANA registry, could lead to ambiguity and stale information, and creates another source of information that may deviate from the registry as new values are assigned or values are deprecated. For the sake of consistency and to support new values while keeping the IANA registries the unique authoritative source of information, the document recommends the use of IANA-maintained YANG modules as the single source of information.

When designing a YANG module for a functionality governed by a protocol for which IANA maintains a registry, it is RECOMMENDED to specify an IANA-maintained module that echoes the content of that registry, rather than including that content in an IETF-maintained module. When one or more registries sit under the same registry group, it is RECOMMENDED to define an IANA-maintained module for each registry, although designers MAY consider a single module covering all of them if maintaining one module is manageable.

An IANA-maintained module may use the identityref data type approach or the enumeration data type approach. Identities are useful if the registry entries are organized hierarchically, possibly including multiple inheritances, and the reasoning for the design choice MUST be documented in the companion specification. Designers MAY supply the initial full version of the module in a specification document, or only a script to be used for generating the module, such as an XSLT stylesheet or a Python script. In both cases the document MUST include a note saying that it is only documenting the initial version of the module and that the authoritative version is to be retrieved from the IANA registry. If an IANA-maintained module is imported by another module, a normative reference with the IANA URL from which to retrieve it SHOULD be included.
sections.plainLanguage: Some registries, such as the list of interface types, are already published in more than one format. The document says to pick one source and keep it in step: if a registry is IANA's, the module that mirrors it should be IANA's too, so that nobody is reading a stale copy.

viz.caption: THE SECTIONS A DOCUMENT WITH YANG MUST HAVE

items.title: Narrative sections
items.text: Must be present, with an overview of the scope and field of application.

items.title: Definitions section
items.text: Must be present, and holds the modules the document defines.

items.title: Security Considerations
items.text: Must be present, and must name the sensitive writable nodes, readable nodes and operations.

items.title: IANA Considerations
items.text: Must be present, with the namespace and the module registration.

items.title: References
items.text: Must be present, with a normative reference for every imported module.

items.title: Terminology section
items.text: Must be present if the document defines or imports any terms.

viz.caption: HOW A NORMATIVE MODULE IS MARKED IN THE DOCUMENT (RFC 9907 SECTION 3.2)

data.title: Code component markers
data.code:
<CODE BEGINS>
file "ietf-foo@2016-03-20.yang"

    module ietf-foo {
      namespace "urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-foo";
      prefix "foo";
      organization "...";
      contact "...";
      description "...";
      revision 2016-03-20 {
        description "Latest revision";
        reference "RFC FFFF: Foo Protocol";
      }
      // ... more statements
    }
<CODE ENDS>

viz.caption: THE NAMING RULES FOR A MODULE AND ITS IDENTIFIERS

items.title: ietf- prefix
items.text: Every normative YANG module published by the IETF begins with it.

items.title: iana- prefix
items.text: Every IANA-maintained YANG module begins with it.

items.title: example- prefix
items.text: Recommended for example modules, which are not normative.

items.title: Unique names
items.text: Published module names are unique, and a name is never reused.

items.title: Identifier length
items.text: Between 1 and 64 characters in published modules.

items.title: Identifier style
items.text: Lowercase letters, numbers and dashes; a list name is singular, its container plural.

viz.caption: WHAT MUST AND WHEN EACH BEHAVE

cells: The data node instances are silently deleted, and this is not an error
The datastore returns a validation error
Conditional model composition with augment or uses, based on static properties
Enforcing a value restriction that involves more than one data node

viz.caption: WHAT THE SECURITY SECTION MUST NAME

items.title: Writable data nodes
items.text: Those that could be especially disruptive if abused, with the risk explained.

items.title: Readable data nodes
items.text: Those holding especially sensitive information or raising privacy concerns, with the reason explained.

items.title: Operations
items.text: YANG rpc statements that are potentially harmful to system behaviour or raise privacy concerns.

items.title: Reused groupings
items.text: A pointer to the security considerations of the document that defines them.

viz.caption: THE RULES FOR AN IANA-MAINTAINED MODULE

items.title: One source of truth
items.text: The module mirrors the registry and is retrieved from IANA, not copied elsewhere.

items.title: One module per registry
items.text: Recommended, though a single module for a whole group is allowed if manageable.

items.title: Identities or enumerations
items.text: Either may be used, and the reason for the choice must be documented.

items.title: Initial version only
items.text: The document states that it records the initial version and the registry holds the current one.
